title: A2 Consolidation
subtitle: Bring every A2 skill together: past, future, and full conversations

lessons.title: Tout au passé
lessons.description: Review the passé composé and imparfait working together in one varied story.

blocks.heading: Passé composé: the backbone of a story
blocks.body: The passé composé tells us WHAT HAPPENED — the events, one after another. Most verbs use avoir + past participle; movement verbs like aller, partir, arriver, and reflexive verbs use être instead, and their participle agrees with the subject.

examples.french: Samedi, je suis parti tôt.
examples.english: On Saturday, I left early.

examples.french: J'ai pris le train de huit heures.
examples.english: I took the eight o'clock train.

examples.french: Nous sommes arrivés à midi.
examples.english: We arrived at noon.

examples.french: Elle a rencontré une amie à la gare.
examples.english: She met a friend at the station.

examples.french: Il a plu pendant une heure.
examples.english: It rained for an hour.

blocks.tip: Ask yourself: is this a single completed event on the timeline? If yes, reach for the passé composé.

blocks.heading: Imparfait: setting the scene
blocks.body: The imparfait paints the BACKGROUND — what things were like, what was going on, what used to happen regularly. Its endings are the same for every verb (except être): -ais, -ais, -ait, -ions, -iez, -aient, added to the nous-form stem.

examples.french: Il faisait beau ce matin-là.
examples.english: The weather was nice that morning.

examples.french: J'étais très fatigué.
examples.english: I was very tired.

examples.french: Il y avait beaucoup de monde dans le train.
examples.english: There were a lot of people on the train.

examples.french: D'habitude, je prenais le bus.
examples.english: Usually, I used to take the bus.

examples.french: Elle portait un manteau bleu.
examples.english: She was wearing a blue coat.

blocks.tip: Description, weather, feelings, ongoing background, and repeated habits almost always call for the imparfait.

blocks.heading: Weaving the two tenses together
blocks.body: In a natural story, the imparfait sets the scene and the passé composé interrupts it with an event — often linked by "quand" or "pendant que". Connectors like "puis", "ensuite", "tout à coup" and "enfin" keep the events moving forward.

examples.french: Je dormais quand le téléphone a sonné.
examples.english: I was sleeping when the phone rang.

examples.french: Pendant qu'il pleuvait, nous avons attendu à l'intérieur.
examples.english: While it was raining, we waited inside.

examples.french: Il faisait nuit ; tout à coup, la lumière s'est éteinte.
examples.english: It was dark; suddenly, the light went out.

examples.french: Puis nous avons raconté toute l'histoire à nos amis.
examples.english: Then we told the whole story to our friends.

blocks.tip: One useful pattern: imparfait = the ongoing action, passé composé = the action that cuts across it.

blocks.heading: Choosing passé composé or imparfait
blocks.body: Ask what job the verb is doing. A completed event, a change, or a reaction → passé composé. A description, an ongoing state, or a habit → imparfait. The two often appear in the very same sentence, each doing its own job.

examples.french: Il faisait beau, alors nous sommes sortis.
examples.english: The weather was nice, so we went out.
examples.note: imparfait = background, passé composé = the resulting action

examples.french: J'avais faim, j'ai donc acheté un sandwich.
examples.english: I was hungry, so I bought a sandwich.

examples.french: Elle était fatiguée mais elle a fini son travail.
examples.english: She was tired but she finished her work.

examples.french: Nous étions en vacances quand il a téléphoné.
examples.english: We were on holiday when he called.

blocks.tip: If you could replace the verb with "was/were + -ing" in English, French usually wants the imparfait.

blocks.heading: Building a complete short narration
blocks.body: A well-told story mixes both tenses with time connectors: start with the scene (imparfait), add the events in order (passé composé + puis/ensuite/enfin), and use "quand" or "pendant que" to interrupt the background with an action.

examples.french: C'était un samedi tranquille. Je lisais un livre quand mon téléphone a sonné.
examples.english: It was a quiet Saturday. I was reading a book when my phone rang.

examples.french: Nous avons pris le train, puis nous avons marché jusqu'à la mer.
examples.english: We took the train, then we walked to the sea.

examples.french: Il pleuvait pendant que nous attendions ; enfin, le bus est arrivé.
examples.english: It was raining while we were waiting; finally, the bus arrived.

blocks.tip: Read your own sentence back: does the imparfait part feel like a photo, and the passé composé part feel like an action? That's the balance you want.

passages.title: Un week-end mouvementé
passages.french: Samedi dernier, il faisait beau et j'étais content de partir en voyage. Je me suis levé tôt, j'ai pris le train de huit heures et je suis arrivé à la gare de Lyon vers midi. Il y avait beaucoup de monde. Pendant que j'attendais un taxi, tout à coup, j'ai rencontré mon ancienne copine de classe, Sophie ! Nous ne nous étions pas vus depuis des années. Nous avons parlé pendant une heure et elle m'a raconté sa nouvelle vie à Lyon. Ensuite, il a commencé à pleuvoir, alors nous sommes entrés dans un café. Malheureusement, j'ai perdu mon téléphone ce jour-là, mais heureusement, un serveur l'a retrouvé. Enfin, le soir, j'étais fatigué mais très heureux de cette journée pleine de surprises.
passages.english: Last Saturday, the weather was nice and I was happy to go on a trip. I got up early, took the eight o'clock train, and arrived at Gare de Lyon around noon. There were a lot of people. While I was waiting for a taxi, all of a sudden, I met my old classmate, Sophie! We hadn't seen each other in years. We talked for an hour and she told me about her new life in Lyon. Then it started to rain, so we went into a café. Unfortunately, I lost my phone that day, but luckily, a waiter found it. Finally, in the evening, I was tired but very happy about this day full of surprises.

lessons.title: Tout au futur
lessons.description: Review futur proche and futur simple together while planning ahead.

blocks.heading: Futur proche: what's coming up soon
blocks.body: The futur proche (aller + infinitive) is the everyday way to talk about near or planned future events — much like English "going to". Conjugate aller in the present, then add the infinitive.

examples.french: Je vais partir demain matin.
examples.english: I'm going to leave tomorrow morning.

examples.french: Tu vas déménager bientôt ?
examples.english: Are you going to move soon?

examples.french: Nous allons voyager en Italie cet été.
examples.english: We're going to travel to Italy this summer.

examples.french: Elle va changer de travail le mois prochain.
examples.english: She's going to change jobs next month.

examples.french: Ils vont se marier l'année prochaine.
examples.english: They're going to get married next year.

blocks.tip: Futur proche feels close and certain — perfect for plans already decided.

blocks.heading: Futur simple: firm plans and predictions
blocks.body: The futur simple adds endings (-ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont) straight onto the infinitive (dropping the final -e for -re verbs). Many common verbs have irregular stems that must be learned: ser- (être), aur- (avoir), fer- (faire), ir- (aller), viendr- (venir), pourr- (pouvoir), voudr- (vouloir), devr- (devoir), saur- (savoir), enverr- (envoyer).

examples.french: Je serai médecin dans cinq ans.
examples.english: I will be a doctor in five years.

examples.french: Nous aurons plus de temps l'année prochaine.
examples.english: We will have more time next year.

examples.french: Elle fera ses études à Paris.
examples.english: She will study in Paris.

examples.french: Tu pourras m'aider samedi ?
examples.english: Will you be able to help me on Saturday?

examples.french: Ils économiseront pour acheter une maison.
examples.english: They will save up to buy a house.

blocks.tip: Regular futur simple: infinitive + ending. "Voyager" → je voyagerai, tu voyageras, elle voyagera...

blocks.heading: Mixing futur proche and futur simple
blocks.body: In everyday speech, French speakers freely mix both futures in the same conversation: futur proche for what's about to happen, futur simple for wider plans, hopes and predictions further off. Time markers like "demain", "bientôt", "un jour" and "dans dix ans" help the listener place events.

examples.french: Demain, je vais chercher un appartement, et un jour, j'aurai enfin mon propre studio.
examples.english: Tomorrow, I'm going to look for an apartment, and one day, I'll finally have my own studio.

examples.french: Nous allons décider ce soir, mais nous n'économiserons pas avant janvier.
examples.english: We're going to decide tonight, but we won't save money before January.

examples.french: Bientôt tu vas voyager, et plus tard, tu réaliseras tous tes projets.
examples.english: Soon you're going to travel, and later, you'll achieve all your plans.

blocks.tip: There's no strict rule — trust the sense: is it close and concrete, or further off and more general?

blocks.heading: Futur proche vs futur simple: which one?
blocks.body: Both futures are correct almost everywhere — the choice is about feel, not strict rule. Futur proche (aller + infinitive) suits near, decided, spoken-style plans. Futur simple suits predictions, promises, formal writing, and anything further off or less certain.

examples.french: Je vais appeler le médecin maintenant.
examples.english: I'm going to call the doctor now.

examples.french: Un jour, la technologie changera tout.
examples.english: One day, technology will change everything.

examples.french: On va manger dans dix minutes.
examples.english: We're going to eat in ten minutes.

examples.french: Je vous enverrai les documents la semaine prochaine.
examples.english: I will send you the documents next week.

blocks.tip: In conversation, futur proche is far more common than futur simple for everyday plans.

blocks.heading: Futur simple: the irregular stems to know by heart
blocks.body: Ten irregular stems cover almost every common verb: être→ser-, avoir→aur-, faire→fer-, aller→ir-, venir→viendr-, pouvoir→pourr-, vouloir→voudr-, devoir→devr-, savoir→saur-, envoyer→enverr-. The endings never change: -ai, -as, -a, -ons, -ez, -ont.

examples.french: Nous serons en retard.
examples.english: We will be late.

examples.french: Vous aurez besoin de vos papiers.
examples.english: You will need your papers.

examples.french: Ils feront le tour du monde.
examples.english: They will travel around the world.

examples.french: Elle ira à l'université l'année prochaine.
examples.english: She will go to university next year.

blocks.tip: Learn the stems as a chant: ser-, aur-, fer-, ir-, viendr-, pourr-, voudr-, devr-, saur-, enverr-.

passages.title: Mes projets pour l'avenir
passages.french: La semaine prochaine, je vais quitter mon travail actuel : j'ai enfin décidé de changer de carrière. Le mois prochain, je vais commencer une formation d'infirmier. Ce sera difficile, mais j'espère y arriver. Dans deux ans, j'obtiendrai mon diplôme et je pourrai enfin travailler dans un hôpital. Bientôt, je vais aussi déménager plus près de l'école. Mes parents m'aideront pendant cette période, et mon frère m'enverra de l'argent si j'en ai besoin. Un jour, je réaliserai mon rêve d'enfance : soigner les gens. Plus tard, je voudrai peut-être étudier à l'étranger. En attendant, je vais économiser un peu chaque mois pour être prêt.
passages.english: Next week, I am going to leave my current job: I have finally decided to change careers. Next month, I am going to start nursing training. It will be difficult, but I hope to manage it. In two years, I will get my diploma and I will finally be able to work in a hospital. Soon, I am also going to move closer to the school. My parents will help me during this period, and my brother will send me money if I need it. One day, I will achieve my childhood dream: caring for people. Later, I might want to study abroad. In the meantime, I am going to save a little each month to be ready.

lessons.title: Conversation complète
lessons.description: Put every A2 skill together in one long, natural conversation.

blocks.heading: Opening a conversation naturally
blocks.body: A real conversation starts with a greeting, a quick check-in, and small talk about what's new — then it flows wherever the speakers take it. "Ça fait longtemps !" and "Quoi de neuf ?" are perfect openers with people you already know.

examples.french: Salut ! Ça fait longtemps qu'on ne s'est pas vus !
examples.english: Hi! It's been a long time since we've seen each other!

examples.french: Quoi de neuf ?
examples.english: What's new?

examples.french: Ça va, et toi ?
examples.english: I'm fine, and you?

blocks.tip: In real French conversation, small talk is not optional — jumping straight to business can feel abrupt.

blocks.heading: Giving opinions and reacting
blocks.body: A2 speakers can already share opinions with simple, useful frames: "à mon avis", "je pense que", "je trouve que". Reactions like "c'est génial", "dommage", "franchement" and "heureusement" keep the conversation alive and personal.

examples.french: À mon avis, c'est une excellente idée.
examples.english: In my opinion, it's an excellent idea.

examples.french: Je trouve que c'est un peu cher.
examples.english: I find that it's a bit expensive.

examples.french: Franchement, je suis très content pour toi !
examples.english: Honestly, I'm very happy for you!

examples.french: C'est dommage, mais heureusement, il y a une autre solution.
examples.english: That's a shame, but fortunately, there's another solution.

blocks.tip: "Par contre" is the everyday way to soften a contrast — much more common in speech than "mais" alone.

blocks.heading: Past, present, and future in one breath
blocks.body: Fluent A2 conversation moves freely between tenses in a single exchange: what happened, how things are now, and what's coming next. Time markers do the heavy lifting — listeners follow the timeline through words like "hier", "maintenant", and "bientôt", not through complicated grammar.

examples.french: Hier, j'ai rencontré un vieil ami, et maintenant on va se revoir bientôt.
examples.english: Yesterday, I met an old friend, and now we're going to see each other again soon.

examples.french: Avant, je détestais mon travail ; par contre, je vais bientôt changer de carrière.
examples.english: Before, I hated my job; on the other hand, I'm going to change careers soon.

examples.french: On se rappelle ce voyage, et un jour, on en refera un autre.
examples.english: We remember that trip, and one day, we'll take another one.

blocks.tip: Don't be afraid to mix tenses in one sentence — that's exactly what natural French conversation sounds like.

blocks.heading: Review: tu or vous in conversation
blocks.body: Before you dive into a conversation, decide your register. "Tu" for friends, family, and people your own age you already know; "vous" for strangers, older people, and professional contexts. Once you choose, stay consistent throughout the whole exchange.

examples.french: Salut ! Tu vas bien ? Qu'est-ce que tu deviens ?
examples.english: Hi! Are you well? What have you been up to?

examples.french: Bonjour, madame. Comment allez-vous ? Vous avez passé un bon week-end ?
examples.english: Hello, ma'am. How are you? Did you have a good weekend?

examples.french: Alors, tu as des nouvelles de ta famille ?
examples.english: So, do you have any news from your family?

blocks.tip: Mixing tu and vous with the same person mid-conversation sounds like a mistake — pick one and keep it.

blocks.heading: Connecting opinion, reason, and reaction
blocks.body: Full conversations link ideas together: state something, give a reason with "parce que", react with an adverb, then pivot to a new topic with "et toi ?" or "au fait". This is how A2 speakers sound genuinely conversational rather than like they're reading a list of sentences.

examples.french: Je suis content, parce que j'ai enfin trouvé un travail.
examples.english: I'm happy, because I finally found a job.

examples.french: Franchement, c'est une excellente nouvelle. Et toi, quoi de neuf ?
examples.english: Honestly, that's excellent news. And you, what's new?

examples.french: Au fait, tu te souviens de notre voyage à Nice ?
examples.english: By the way, do you remember our trip to Nice?

blocks.tip: "Au fait" (by the way) is a natural way to change subject without sounding abrupt.

passages.title: Retrouvailles au café
passages.french:
— Léa ! Salut ! Ça fait longtemps qu'on ne s'est pas vues !
— Salut Marc ! Quoi de neuf ? Tu as l'air en pleine forme !
— Merci ! En fait, j'ai changé de travail le mois dernier. Avant, je détestais mon poste, mais maintenant, je suis vraiment content.
— C'est génial ! Et comment ça s'est passé ?
— Eh bien, j'ai envoyé beaucoup de candidatures, puis on m'a enfin appelé pour un entretien. J'étais très nerveux, mais tout s'est bien passé.
— À mon avis, tu as fait le bon choix. Et pour l'avenir, tu as des projets ?
— Oui ! Je vais déménager près de mon nouveau bureau, et l'année prochaine, j'espère voyager en Asie.
— Franchement, je suis très heureuse pour toi. Moi, je pars en vacances la semaine prochaine.
— Super ! On devrait se revoir avant ton départ.
— D'accord, à bientôt alors !
passages.english:
— Léa! Hi! It's been a long time since we've seen each other!
— Hi Marc! What's new? You look great!
— Thanks! Actually, I changed jobs last month. Before, I hated my position, but now, I'm really happy.
— That's great! And how did it go?
— Well, I sent a lot of applications, then I was finally called for an interview. I was very nervous, but everything went well.
— In my opinion, you made the right choice. And for the future, do you have any plans?
— Yes! I'm going to move near my new office, and next year, I hope to travel to Asia.
— Honestly, I'm very happy for you. As for me, I'm going on holiday next week.
— Great! We should see each other again before you leave.
— OK, see you soon then!
